claim: Klebsiella pneumoniae ATCC 43816 exhibits bacterial persistence against lytic phage Kp11, with a small fraction (~10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁶) surviving phage treatment.
source: In analogy with the concept of antibiotic persistence, the majority of bacteria were rapidly eliminated following lytic phage treatment, while a small fraction (~10–5 to 10–6) survived, resulting in a bi-phasic killing curve (Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing survival fractions and bi-phasic killing curves in Figure 1b.

claim: Descendants of phage persisters show comparable survival fractions to the ancestral population, indicating survival is due to phenotypic heterogeneity rather than genetic mutation.
source: Subsequent killing experiments on the descendants of persisters revealed a comparable survival fraction to the ancestral population, suggesting that this survival was not attributable to genetic mutation but rather to phenotypic heterogeneity, that is phage persistence (Figure 1c).
evidence: Experimental data from killing experiments on persister descendants (Figure 1c) showing no significant difference in survival fractions supports this claim.

claim: The high antibiotic persistence E. coli strain metG* does not exhibit enhanced survival when exposed to lytic phage T4 compared to its ancestor KLY.
source: The observed similar survival rates suggested that increased lag time does not confer protection against phage infection (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Experimental data comparing survival rates of KLY and metG* strains under T4 phage infection (Figure 1d) supports this claim.

claim: Previous studies showed that the high antibiotic persistence E. coli strain hipA7 did not exhibit enhanced survival when exposed to lytic phages compared to its sensitive ancestor.
source: However, previous studies showed that the high antibiotic persistence Escherichia coli strain hipA7 did not exhibit enhanced survival when exposed to lytic phages compared to its sensitive ancestor (Pearl et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pearl et al., 2008.

claim: Heat pre-treatment at elevated temperatures significantly reduces K. pneumoniae's susceptibility to lytic phage Kp11 infection.
source: Remarkably, pre-treatment at elevated temperatures significantly reduced K. pneumonia's susceptibility to lytic phage infection (Figure 2a).
evidence: Experimental data from plaque-forming unit assays (Figure 2a) showing reduced susceptibility after heat treatment supports this claim.

claim: Heat-treated K. pneumoniae bacteria exhibit a reduced killing rate following phage exposure.
source: Killing assays revealed that heat-treated bacteria exhibited a reduced killing rate following phage exposure (Figure 2b), with effects being both time- and temperature-dependent (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental killing assay data (Figure 2b) demonstrating reduced killing rates in heat-treated bacteria supports this claim.

claim: The effects of heat-induced phage tolerance are both time- and temperature-dependent.
source: Killing assays revealed that heat-treated bacteria exhibited a reduced killing rate following phage exposure (Figure 2b), with effects being both time- and temperature-dependent (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data showing dose-response relationships with treatment duration and temperature (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) supports this claim.

claim: Heat-treated bacteria relapse more frequently under phage infection, suggesting a higher probability of resistance mutant emergence.
source: Moreover, infection curves indicated that heat-treated bacteria relapsed more frequently, suggesting a higher probability of resistance mutant emergence (Figure 2c).
evidence: Growth dynamics data (Figure 2c) showing bacterial regrowth in heat-treated cultures supports this claim.

claim: Heat treatment does not directly increase the fraction of phage-resistant mutants in K. pneumoniae populations.
source: Our analysis revealed a negligible presence of resistant mutants in both groups (Figure 2d). Consistent with this, mutation rates estimated using Delbrück-Luria tests (Luria and Delbrück, 1943) confirmed no significant difference (Figure 2e).
evidence: Experimental data from plating assays (Figure 2d) and fluctuation tests (Figure 2e) showing no significant difference in resistant mutant frequencies supports this claim.

claim: The enhanced defense against phage infection following heat treatment reflects a phenotypic boost in survival analogous to antibiotic persistence rather than an increase in phage-resistant mutants.
source: These findings indicated that the enhanced defense against phage infection observed following heat treatment was not due to an increase in phage-resistant mutants, but rather reflected a phenotypic boost in survival analogous to antibiotic persistence (Brauner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no increase in resistant mutants and by citation to antibiotic persistence literature (Brauner et al., 2016).

claim: Heat treatment promotes the emergence of phage resistance by allowing bacteria to undergo more division events under phage pressure.
source: This indicates that the tolerance induced by heat treatment facilitates the emergence and evolution of phage resistance, as heat-treated bacteria underwent more division events under phage pressure, ultimately increasing the likelihood of developing phage resistance (Levin-Reisman et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data (Figure 2g) showing cell division under phage pressure and by citations to resistance evolution literature (Levin-Reisman et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020).

claim: Heat-treated K. pneumoniae bacteria can divide under phage pressure, while untreated bacteria are lysed before dividing.
source: Microscopic observations further revealed that heat-treated bacteria could divide under phage pressure, while untreated bacteria were lysed by phages before dividing (Figure 2g and Figure 2—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Microscopic time-lapse imaging data (Figure 2g) showing differential cell fates supports this claim.

claim: Heat treatment induces phage tolerance in multiple phage-bacteria systems, including K. pneumoniae with phages Kp7, Kp9, Kp10, and Kp11, and E. coli with phages T1 and T4.
source: We next assessed the infection of K. pneumoniae by phages Kp7, Kp9, Kp10, and Kp11 (Huang et al., 2024), as well as E. coli by phages T1 and T4, following pre-heat treatment. Our results revealed a consistent tolerance response across these experiments (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: Experimental data from multiple phage-bacteria combinations (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b) showing consistent tolerance responses supports this claim.

claim: Clinical K. pneumoniae strains K359 and K381 exhibit reduced phage sensitivity following heat treatment.
source: This observation was further validated using clinical K. pneumoniae strains K359 and K381, both of which exhibited a marked reduction in phage sensitivity post-heat treatment (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Experimental data from clinical isolates (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) showing reduced phage sensitivity after heat treatment supports this claim.

claim: Heat-treated bacteria exhibit reduced sensitivity to combined phage treatments.
source: In light of this, we extended our investigation to phage combinations and found that heat-treated bacteria exhibited reduced sensitivity even to combined phage treatments (Figure 3d).
evidence: Experimental data from phage combination experiments (Figure 3d) showing reduced sensitivity in heat-treated bacteria supports this claim.

claim: Heat treatment does not alter the phage adsorption rate to K. pneumoniae.
source: Our analysis revealed that heat treatment did not alter the phage adsorption rate (Figure 4a).
evidence: Experimental adsorption assay data (Figure 4a) showing no significant difference in adsorption rates supports this claim.

claim: Heat treatment does not change the production and structure of the bacterial capsule in K. pneumoniae.
source: Additionally, the production and structure of the bacterial capsule, the primary receptor for phage Kp11, remained unchanged (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data from uronic acid quantification and TEM imaging (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing no change in capsule production or structure supports this claim.

claim: Heat treatment significantly impairs the entry of phage DNA into K. pneumoniae bacteria.
source: However, we observed a significant impairment in the entry of phage DNA into heat-treated bacteria (Figure 4b), suggesting a hindrance in the DNA injection process.
evidence: Experimental qPCR data (Figure 4b) showing reduced phage DNA levels in heat-treated bacteria supports this claim.

claim: Down-regulated proteins in heat-treated K. pneumoniae are predominantly associated with the bacterial envelope.
source: To explore this further, we employed liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) for total protein analysis and identified that the down-regulated proteins were predominantly associated with the bacterial envelope (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data and gene ontology analysis (Figure 4c and d) showing enrichment of envelope-associated proteins among down-regulated proteins supports this claim.

claim: Heat-treated K. pneumoniae bacteria show substantial changes in susceptibility to various envelope stresses, including pH changes, metals, bile salts, and polymyxins.
source: To investigate this, we examined the response of heat-treated bacteria to various envelope stresses, including unfavorable conditions such as pH changes and exposure to toxic compounds (metals, bile salts, and polymyxins), and found substantial changes in susceptibility (Figure 4e).
evidence: Experimental data from stress susceptibility assays (Figure 4e) showing altered survival under various conditions supports this claim.

claim: Heat-treated K. pneumoniae bacteria exhibit increased survival against polymyxins.
source: Interestingly, heat-treated bacteria exhibited increased survival against polymyxins, similar to phage tolerance (Figure 4e).
evidence: Experimental data from polymyxin survival assays (Figure 4e) showing increased survival in heat-treated bacteria supports this claim.

claim: Heat-treated K. pneumoniae bacteria show significantly reduced lipopolysaccharide (LPS) production.
source: Notably, heat-treated bacteria showed significantly reduced lipopolysaccharide (LPS) production, known to mediate polymyxin adsorption (Yin et al., 2020; Figure 4f).
evidence: Experimental data from chromogenic LAL endotoxin assays (Figure 4f) showing reduced LPS levels and citation to polymyxin-LPS interaction literature (Yin et al., 2020) supports this claim.

claim: Bacterial survival under polymyxin treatment increases with LPS reduction.
source: Further experiments using the LPS inhibitor CHIR-090 confirmed that bacterial survival under polymyxin treatment increased with LPS reduction (Figure 4g).
evidence: Experimental data using LPS inhibitor (Figure 4g) showing increased survival with reduced LPS supports this claim.

claim: The evolved mutant BC2G11C1 exhibits significantly enhanced survival following heat treatment.
source: In line with our hypothesis, we identified two distinct mutants, BC2G11C1 and BC3G11C2, which exhibited significantly enhanced survival following heat treatment (Figure 5b).
evidence: Experimental data from heat survival assays (Figure 5b) showing enhanced survival in evolved strains supports this claim.

claim: The evolved mutant BC2G11C1 shows significantly reduced susceptibility to phage infection.
source: However, only BC2G11C1 showed significantly reduced susceptibility to phage infection (Figure 5c).
evidence: Experimental data from efficiency of plating assays (Figure 5c) showing reduced phage susceptibility in BC2G11C1 supports this claim.

claim: The BC2G11C1 mutant maintains growth under phage treatment, indicating phage resistance.
source: Moreover, this strain maintained growth under phage treatment, indicating that the mutation conferred phage resistance (Figure 5d and e).
evidence: Experimental data from killing assays and plating experiments (Figure 5d and e) showing sustained growth and colony formation under phage pressure supports this claim.

claim: The BC2G11C1 mutant acquired both phage resistance and heat tolerance.
source: Thus, the BC2G11C1 mutant acquired both phage resistance and heat tolerance.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing both enhanced heat survival (Figure 5b) and phage resistance (Figure 5c-e).

claim: The phage-resistant mutant BC2G11C1 harbors a truncation in the pspA gene.
source: Whole-genome sequencing of the evolved strains revealed a truncation in the pspA gene in the phage-resistant mutant, which was responsible for the reduced sensitivity to both heat and phage treatment.
evidence: Whole-genome sequencing data (Figure 5f) identifying the pspA truncation mutation supports this claim.

claim: The evolved mutant BC3G11C2 harbors a mutation in the rpoH gene, which confers heat tolerance but does not affect phage resistance.
source: In contrast, the other strain harbored a mutation in the rpoH gene, which conferred heat tolerance but did not affect phage resistance (Figure 5f).
evidence: Whole-genome sequencing data (Figure 5f) and phenotypic characterization showing heat tolerance without phage resistance supports this claim.

claim: The pspA mutation in BC2G11C1 is a gain-of-function mutation.
source: The absence of similar phenotypes in the pspA knockout strain (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) suggested that this was a gain-of-function mutation in the pspA gene. This was further supported by the failure to restore the phenotypes upon reintroduction of the wild type pspA gene into the mutant strain; however, overexpression of the mutated pspA gene in the ancestral strain exhibited a similar phenotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data from knockout and complementation experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) showing that the mutation is gain-of-function supports this claim.

claim: Phage shock proteins encoded by the psp operon are induced by both heat stress and phage infection.
source: Phage shock proteins, encoded by the psp operon, are reported to be induced by both heat stress and phage infection (Flores-Kim and Darwin, 2016; Model et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on phage shock proteins (Flores-Kim and Darwin, 2016; Model et al., 1997).

claim: Phage adsorption to the pspA* mutant is significantly impaired.
source: Adsorption assays revealed a significant impairment in phage adsorption to pspA*, suggesting alterations in receptor availability (Figure 6a).
evidence: Experimental adsorption assay data (Figure 6a) showing reduced phage adsorption to pspA* mutant supports this claim.

claim: The pspA* mutant shows a reduction in capsular production.
source: Further analysis corroborated this observation, demonstrating a reduction in capsular production (Figure 6b) and a complete loss of capsular structure (Figure 6c).
evidence: Experimental data from uronic acid quantification (Figure 6b) showing reduced capsule production supports this claim.

claim: The pspA* mutant exhibits a complete loss of capsular structure.
source: Further analysis corroborated this observation, demonstrating a reduction in capsular production (Figure 6b) and a complete loss of capsular structure (Figure 6c).
evidence: TEM imaging data (Figure 6c) showing absence of capsule structure in pspA* mutant supports this claim.

claim: The pspA* mutant is rapidly cleared from mouse blood, demonstrating a significant reduction in immune evasion capacity.
source: The results showed that pspA* was rapidly cleared from mouse blood, demonstrating a significant reduction in immune evasion capacity (Figure 6d, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: In vivo mouse infection data (Figure 6d, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) showing rapid bacterial clearance from blood supports this claim.

claim: Heat-treated K. pneumoniae bacteria show a mild reduction in immune evasion capacity.
source: A mild reduction in immune evasion was also observed in heat-treated bacteria (Figure 6d).
evidence: In vivo mouse infection data (Figure 6d) showing reduced bacterial persistence in blood for heat-treated bacteria supports this claim.

claim: The pspA* mutant exhibits increased survival to polymyxin treatment without a corresponding increase in minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC).
source: Notably, the pspA* mutant exhibited increased survival to polymyxin treatment (Figure 6e) without a corresponding increase in the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) (Figure 6f), suggesting a tolerant phenotype mediated by a reduction in LPS.
evidence: Experimental data from survival assays (Figure 6e) and disk diffusion assays (Figure 6f) showing increased survival without MIC change supports this claim.

claim: Many down-regulated proteins in the pspA* mutant are envelope-associated.
source: Mass spectrometry analysis indicated that many down-regulated proteins in pspA* were envelope-associated (Figure 6g), implying an important role for the pspA gene in maintaining envelope integrity.
evidence: Mass spectrometry data (Figure 6g) showing enrichment of envelope proteins among down-regulated proteins in pspA* mutant supports this claim.

claim: The pspA gene plays an important role in maintaining envelope integrity.
source: Mass spectrometry analysis indicated that many down-regulated proteins in pspA* were envelope-associated (Figure 6g), implying an important role for the pspA gene in maintaining envelope integrity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from mass spectrometry data (Figure 6g) showing envelope protein changes in pspA* mutant.

claim: Antibiotic persistence confers a distinct advantage to lysogenic phages but does not protect bacteria from lytic phages.
source: Previous reports have demonstrated that antibiotic persistence confers a distinct advantage to lysogenic phages but does not protect bacteria from lytic phages (Pearl et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pearl et al., 2008.

claim: Heat stress enhances phage tolerance, subsequently promoting the emergence of resistance, aligned with observations in antibiotic research.
source: Notably, our research revealed that heat stress enhances phage tolerance, subsequently promoting the emergence of resistance, aligned with observations in antibiotic research (Levin-Reisman et al., 2019; Levin-Reisman et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript and citations to antibiotic tolerance-resistance literature (Levin-Reisman et al., 2019; Levin-Reisman et al., 2017).

claim: Lytic phages can induce antibiotic persistence.
source: In line with recent work by Fernández-García et al., 2024, which showed that lytic phages can induce antibiotic persistence, our findings further highlight the existence of phage persistence, adding depth to bacterial survival strategies and reinforcing the complexity of phage therapy.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fernández-García et al., 2024.

claim: Heat induces protein misfolding and aggregation in bacteria.
source: Heat, as a universal stress, induces protein misfolding and aggregation, despite the activation of heat shock proteins that mitigate these effects (Feder and Hofmann, 1999; Mogk et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to heat stress literature (Feder and Hofmann, 1999; Mogk et al., 2019) and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: The accumulation of misfolded envelope proteins can become toxic, leading to cell death.
source: The accumulation of misfolded envelope proteins can become toxic, leading to cell death (Balchin et al., 2016; Konovalova et al., 2016; Takai et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to protein folding and toxicity literature (Balchin et al., 2016; Konovalova et al., 2016; Takai et al., 1998).

claim: Envelope proteins have relatively low efficiency of translocation and assembly, rendering them more vulnerable under heat treatment.
source: Correspondingly, the relatively low efficiency of translocation and assembly of envelope proteins (Bakkes et al., 2010; Dalbey and Kuhn, 2012; Vigh et al., 2007) renders them more vulnerable under heat treatment (Schiffrin et al., 2017), resulting in a decrease in abundance.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to envelope protein biogenesis literature (Bakkes et al., 2010; Dalbey and Kuhn, 2012; Vigh et al., 2007; Schiffrin et al., 2017).

claim: The reduction in envelope protein abundance under heat treatment might be an adaptive response to elevated temperatures.
source: This reduction in envelope protein might be an adaptive response to elevated temperatures, as evidenced by the observations following heat treatment.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observed reduction in envelope proteins and the phenotypic consequences.

claim: Heat shock potentiates aminoglycosides against Gram-negative bacteria by enhancing antibiotic uptake and promoting protein aggregation.
source: Recent studies have shown that heat shock potentiates aminoglycosides against Gram-negative bacteria by enhancing antibiotic uptake and promoting protein aggregation (Lv et al., 2023), indicating that heat stress can contribute to bacterial sensitivity to antibiotics, which could also extend to phages in our study.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lv et al., 2023.

claim: PspA is a key regulator in the phage shock protein system that functions as part of the envelope stress response system in bacteria.
source: PspA, a key regulator in the phage shock protein system, functions as part of the envelope stress response system in bacteria, preventing membrane depolarization and ensuring the envelope stability (Flores-Kim and Darwin, 2016; Horstman and Darwin, 2012; Kleerebezem and Tommassen, 1993; Yamaguchi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to PspA function literature (Flores-Kim and Darwin, 2016; Horstman and Darwin, 2012; Kleerebezem and Tommassen, 1993; Yamaguchi et al., 2010).

claim: PspA is analogous to ESCRT-III, a component of the ESCRT machinery in eukaryotic cells involved in membrane remodeling.
source: Recent studies have shown that PspA is analogous to ESCRT-III, a component of the ESCRT machinery in eukaryotic cells, which plays a crucial role in membrane remodeling (Junglas et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to PspA-ESCRT literature (Junglas et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021).

claim: The bacterial envelope serves as a barrier against environmental stresses.
source: The bacterial envelope acts both as a defense barrier against external stresses and as a conduit for invaders. While it reduces the invasion of harmful substances and maintains intra-extracellular balance (Arts et al., 2015; Raivio, 2014; Wood, 2015), it also provides contacts for invaders; for example, capsules serve as receptors for phages (Latka et al., 2021), and LPS interacts with polymyxins (Manioglu et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to bacterial envelope function literature (Arts et al., 2015; Raivio, 2014; Wood, 2015).

claim: Capsules serve as receptors for phages.
source: The bacterial envelope acts both as a defense barrier against external stresses and as a conduit for invaders. While it reduces the invasion of harmful substances and maintains intra-extracellular balance (Arts et al., 2015; Raivio, 2014; Wood, 2015), it also provides contacts for invaders; for example, capsules serve as receptors for phages (Latka et al., 2021), and LPS interacts with polymyxins (Manioglu et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to phage receptor literature (Latka et al., 2021).

claim: LPS interacts with polymyxins.
source: The bacterial envelope acts both as a defense barrier against external stresses and as a conduit for invaders. While it reduces the invasion of harmful substances and maintains intra-extracellular balance (Arts et al., 2015; Raivio, 2014; Wood, 2015), it also provides contacts for invaders; for example, capsules serve as receptors for phages (Latka et al., 2021), and LPS interacts with polymyxins (Manioglu et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to polymyxin-LPS interaction literature (Manioglu et al., 2022).

claim: Heat-induced alteration to the bacterial envelope could be a double-edged sword, affecting both phage susceptibility and host immune interactions.
source: Thus, heat-induced alteration to the envelope could be a double-edged sword. Clinically, heat stress would not only impact phage susceptibility but also alter the interaction between K. pneumoniae and the host immune system.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing both reduced phage susceptibility and impaired immune evasion in heat-treated bacteria.

claim: Increased sensitivity to acidic conditions and bile salts induced by heat stress challenges bacterial survival at K. pneumoniae colonization sites in the human body.
source: Furthermore, increased sensitivity to acidic conditions and bile salts induced by heat stress challenges bacterial survival, particularly relevant to K. pneumoniae colonization sites in the human body (Gasink et al., 2009; Martin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (Figure 4e) showing increased sensitivity to pH and bile salts, and citations to K. pneumoniae colonization literature (Gasink et al., 2009; Martin et al., 2016).

claim: Even moderately elevated temperatures, such as 42°C, can induce phage tolerance with prolonged treatment.
source: We found that heat-induced phage tolerance is both time- and temperature-dependent; even moderately elevated temperatures, such as 42 °C, can induce phage tolerance with prolonged treatment, indicating alterations in the bacterial envelope.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showing temperature and time-dependent effects.

claim: Elevated body temperature, akin to fever, may affect bacterial survival and colonization by modulating their responses to the host immune system and antimicrobial agents.
source: This suggests that elevated body temperature, akin to fever, may affect bacterial survival and colonization by modulating their responses to the host immune system and antimicrobial agents.
evidence: The claim is speculative, extrapolating from experimental heat treatment data to physiological fever conditions.

claim: Elevated temperatures alter life-history traits in phage communities.
source: Since elevated temperatures also alter life-history traits in phage communities (Greenrod et al., 2024), they may similarly impact bacterial responses to heat stress, phage, and antibiotic treatments, underscoring the need for further research into the role of fever in bacterial growth and survival during therapy.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Greenrod et al., 2024.

claim: Phage Kp11 is a lytic phage with GenBank accession number ON148528.1.
source: To address this question, we investigated the killing dynamics of Klebsiella pneumoniae under treatment with the lytic phage Kp11 (GenBank: ON148528.1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Huang et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by GenBank accession information and citation to Huang et al., 2024.

claim: The bacterial capsule is the primary receptor for phage Kp11.
source: Additionally, the production and structure of the bacterial capsule, the primary receptor for phage Kp11, remained unchanged (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the context of the study.

claim: Phages typically require a secondary receptor, often an outer membrane component, to establish adsorption and initiate DNA injection.
source: In addition to a primary receptor, phages typically require a secondary receptor, often an outer membrane component (Sueki et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2006), to establish adsorption and initiate DNA injection.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to phage receptor literature (Sueki et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2006).

claim: Polymyxin is a last-resort antibiotic for treating carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae.
source: Given that polymyxin is a last-resort antibiotic for treating carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae, this cross-tolerance with phages might present a significant challenge to already scarce treatment options.
evidence: The claim represents established clinical knowledge about polymyxin use.

claim: K. pneumoniae capsules play a critical role in evading host immunity during septicemia.
source: Given the critical role of K. pneumoniae capsules in evading host immunity during septicemia (Huang et al., 2022), we assessed the immune evasion capacity of the pspA* mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2022.

claim: Antibiotic tolerance can promote the evolution of antibiotic resistance.
source: Beyond resistance, antibiotic tolerance presents a critical concern, enabling bacteria to survive high concentrations of antibiotics (Balaban et al., 2019; Balaban et al., 2004; Brauner et al., 2016), which can further promote the evolution of resistance (Levin-Reisman et al., 2019; Levin-Reisman et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to antibiotic tolerance and resistance evolution literature (Levin-Reisman et al., 2019; Levin-Reisman et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020).

claim: Phage therapy often involves combining multiple phages to minimize the risk of resistance evolution.
source: Phage therapy often involves combining multiple phages to minimize the risk of resistance evolution (Chan and Abedon, 2012; León and Bastías, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to phage therapy literature (Chan and Abedon, 2012; León and Bastías, 2015).

claim: The Kp7-resistant strain RKp7 remained susceptible to phage Kp11.
source: Notably, we identified a Kp7-resistant strain, RKp7, which remained susceptible to Kp11 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a) and was also sensitive to the combination of Kp7 and Kp11 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: Experimental data from plating assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a) showing RKp7 sensitivity to Kp11 supports this claim.

claim: Combination therapy with Kp7 and Kp11 is effective against spontaneous resistance-conferring mutations to a single phage.
source: This approved the effectiveness of combination therapy against spontaneous resistance-conferring mutations to a single phage (León and Bastías, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b) and citation to León and Bastías, 2015.

claim: After heat treatment, phage combination therapy has a much higher propensity to fail due to the evolution of resistance to both phages.
source: Intriguingly, however, post heat treatment, the combination had a much higher propensity to fail due to the evolution of resistance to both phages (Figure 3d).
evidence: Experimental data from turbid well assays (Figure 3d) showing increased resistance emergence in heat-treated bacteria under combination therapy supports this claim.

claim: Bacterial persistence against phages is characterized by heterogeneous survival, analogous to antibiotic persistence.
source: Here, using Klebsiella pneumoniae ATCC 43816 and its lytic phage Kp11 as a model system, we investigated bacterial persistence against phages, characterized by heterogeneous survival, analogous to antibiotic persistence.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing bi-phasic killing curves and phenotypic heterogeneity (Figure 1b, 1c).

claim: Heat treatment leads to a reduction in envelope components, thereby inhibiting phage DNA injection.
source: Further experiments demonstrated that heat stress leads to a reduction in envelope components, thereby inhibiting phage DNA injection.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 4c, 4d) and phage DNA injection assays (Figure 4b).

claim: Heat-induced reduction in envelope components results in systematic alterations in envelope stress responses, rendering bacteria tolerant to polymyxin while making them hypersensitive to pH changes and immune clearance.
source: Additionally, this heat-induced reduction resulted in systematic alterations in envelope stress responses, rendering bacteria tolerant to the antibiotic polymyxin while making them hypersensitive to pH changes and immune clearance.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing altered stress responses (Figure 4e) and immune evasion (Figure 6d).

claim: Antibiotic resistance poses a significant threat to global public health.
source: Antibiotic resistance poses a significant threat to global public health, emphasizing the urgent need for innovative strategies to combat bacterial infections (Luong et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Luong et al., 2020 and represents established scientific consensus.

claim: Phage therapy has emerged as a promising alternative to antibiotics.
source: Phage therapy has emerged as a promising alternative, yet the rapid emergence of phage-resistant bacterial mutants challenges its effectiveness (Oechslin, 2018; Salmond and Fineran, 2015; Strathdee et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to phage therapy literature (Oechslin, 2018; Salmond and Fineran, 2015; Strathdee et al., 2023).

claim: The rapid emergence of phage-resistant bacterial mutants challenges the effectiveness of phage therapy.
source: Phage therapy has emerged as a promising alternative, yet the rapid emergence of phage-resistant bacterial mutants challenges its effectiveness (Oechslin, 2018; Salmond and Fineran, 2015; Strathdee et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to phage therapy literature (Oechslin, 2018; Salmond and Fineran, 2015; Strathdee et al., 2023).

claim: Antibiotic tolerance enables bacteria to survive high concentrations of antibiotics.
source: Beyond resistance, antibiotic tolerance presents a critical concern, enabling bacteria to survive high concentrations of antibiotics (Balaban et al., 2019; Balaban et al., 2004; Brauner et al., 2016), which can further promote the evolution of resistance (Levin-Reisman et al., 2019; Levin-Reisman et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to antibiotic tolerance literature (Balaban et al., 2019; Balaban et al., 2004; Brauner et al., 2016).

claim: Canonical antibiotic persistence is characterized by an extended lag time or slow growth rate.
source: Canonical antibiotic persistence is characterized by an extended lag time or slow growth rate (Balaban et al., 2004; Brauner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to antibiotic persistence literature (Balaban et al., 2004; Brauner et al., 2016).

claim: Antibiotic persistence can be triggered by stresses such as starvation.
source: Given that antibiotic persistence can be triggered by stresses such as starvation (Betts et al., 2002; Nguyen et al., 2011), we explored whether phage persistence might similarly be affected or not.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to antibiotic persistence literature (Betts et al., 2002; Nguyen et al., 2011).
